passages.happening:
‘Hear this word, you cows of Bashan on Mount Samaria, you women who oppress the poor and crush the needy’ (verse 1), who tell their husbands to bring them more to drink.

The Lord GOD has sworn by his holiness that days are coming when they will be taken away with hooks, and those after them with fishhooks (verse 2). They will go out through the broken walls, each one straight ahead, and be cast out toward Harmon (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Samaria under Jeroboam II was home to a wealthy class whose comfort depended on the produce and labor of the countryside. Inscribed potsherds found at Samaria, the Samaria ostraca, usually dated to the first half of the eighth century BC, record shipments of wine and oil from estates to officials in the capital. The women Amos addresses belonged to this privileged circle.

Bashan, the fertile plateau east of the Sea of Galilee, was famous for its rich pastures and well-fed cattle. To call the women cows of Bashan pictured them as sleek, pampered and heavy with good living. God swears by his holiness, the most solemn oath there is.

The hooks may reflect the way captives were led away, sometimes by ropes or hooks, as Assyrian carvings show prisoners; others think the pictures come from fishing or from a butcher's hooks. Harmon is unknown, a place name or a copyist's form of another name, and translations vary. The exile came when Assyria deported much of the north after 722 BC.
passages.later: Bashan's fat cattle were a byword (Deuteronomy 32:14; Psalm 22:12). Isaiah spoke just as bluntly to the proud women of Jerusalem (Isaiah 3:16-26) and to the men who drank from morning to night (Isaiah 5:11-12).
passages.hard:
Is it demeaning for Amos to call women cows of Bashan?

The insult is sharp, and it is meant to be. Several things put it in context. Bashan's cattle were famous for their quality and fatness, so the picture is about pampered comfort, not ugliness. The women are condemned not for being women but for what they do: they oppress the poor and crush the needy, and push their husbands for more luxury. Amos is just as hard on men throughout the book, the judges who take bribes, the merchants who cheat, the rich lounging on ivory beds, and other prophets speak as bluntly about the powerful of both sexes. Some interpreters also think the phrase may come from religious language tied to Bashan, though that is uncertain.

Readers may still feel the harshness, and that is part of Amos's purpose. He uses shocking language to break through the comfort of people who did not see what it cost others. It is a word against oppression, and it gives no one a license to speak of women with contempt.
passages.asks: The women's comfort was paid for by the poor. Ask whose labor stands behind your own comforts, and whether you have ever asked. And ask what it would take for you to hear a hard word as meant for you.

passages.happening:
Amos mimics a priest's call to worship. “Go to Bethel and transgress; rebel even more at Gilgal! Bring your sacrifices every morning, your tithes every three days” (verse 4).

Offer leavened bread as a thank offering, and announce your freewill offerings loudly, ‘For that is what you children of Israel love to do,’ declares the Lord GOD (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
These two verses are irony. A priest would invite worshipers to come to the sanctuary and worship. Amos invites them to come and sin. Bethel and Gilgal were the great pilgrimage shrines of the north.

The law called for tithes each year and a special tithe every third year. Amos's every three days exaggerates the worshipers' zeal to expose it. Thank offerings could include leavened bread, and freewill offerings were voluntary gifts. To announce them loudly turned devotion into a show. The people loved their religion. They did not love God's ways.
passages.later: The law set out the yearly tithe and the tithe of the third year for the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow (Deuteronomy 14:22-29). Thank offerings could be brought with leavened bread (Leviticus 7:13).
passages.asks: The worshipers loved to be seen giving. Ask what part of your religious life you do mostly because you like doing it, or being seen doing it. And ask what God might say about worship that leaves your treatment of others unchanged.

passages.happening:
God lists the warnings he has sent. He gave them ‘cleanness of teeth’, empty mouths in every town, ‘yet you did not return to Me,’ declares the LORD (verse 6). He withheld rain three months before harvest, sent rain on one town and not another, and people staggered from town to town for water (verses 7-8). He struck their gardens with blight and mildew, and locusts ate their figs and olives (verse 9). He sent plague and the sword (verse 10). He overthrew some of them like Sodom and Gomorrah, and they were like a burning stick snatched from the fire (verse 11). Each time comes the same line: they did not return.

So God will act, and the summons is ‘prepare to meet your God, O Israel’ (verse 12). The LORD is the one ‘who forms the mountains, who creates the wind and reveals His thoughts to man’ (verse 13), who turns dawn to darkness, and the LORD God of Hosts is his name.
passages.hearers:
The poem of verses 6 to 11 has five stanzas naming seven disasters: famine, drought, blight, locusts, plague, the sword, and overthrow. Each closes with the same line, that they did not return to God, like a sad drumbeat. The disasters cannot be tied to particular years, but all of them were familiar in Israel's recent memory, and Israel had suffered badly in wars with Aram in the late ninth century. They follow closely the covenant warnings Israel accepted at Sinai.

Cleanness of teeth is a vivid way of saying famine: there is nothing to chew. Verse 12 leaves the punishment unnamed, ‘that is what I will do to you’, which makes it more ominous. Then it summons Israel to prepare to meet its God.

Verse 13 is the first of three hymns in Amos praising God as creator (see also 5:8-9 and 9:5-6). Some scholars think these were added later; others see them as Amos's own use of familiar hymns. The God Israel must meet made the mountains and the wind.
passages.later: The law had warned of drought, blight and plague for a people who broke the covenant (Leviticus 26:19-26; Deuteronomy 28:22). Zechariah later used the picture of the burning stick: “Is not this man a firebrand snatched from the fire?” (Zechariah 3:2).
passages.hard:
Does this chapter mean that every famine, drought or plague is God's punishment?

Amos says that God sent these warnings to Israel, and that Israel did not listen. He stands inside the covenant Israel had made at Sinai, which named these troubles as its warnings, and he speaks as a prophet given God's word about a particular people at a particular time. The chapter's point is the refusal: God called again and again, and they did not return.

It gives no one the right to read their own drought, illness or loss, or anyone else's, as a punishment. Scripture itself resists that reading, in Job and in Jesus' own words.

A word for anyone who has lived through a flood, a storm or another disaster. Your loss was not a judgment on you. When Jesus was asked about people killed when a tower fell, he refused that reading of a disaster: “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you are carrying this, you need people more than explanations. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page has people you can call.
passages.asks: Five times God says that they did not return to him. Ask where God has been calling you and you have not turned. And ask what it would mean to prepare to meet your God, not with fear only, but with a changed life.
